w: Venice's real main street has no pavement - a 3.8-kilometre reverse-S of water, 30 to 90 metres wide, threading from the railway station end of the lagoon down to the San Marco basin. Every gondola, vaporetto and delivery barge in the city answers to its curve. Depth: a modest five metres. Traffic: relentless.
s: Venice's real main street, and it's made of water
_facts: Largest channel in Venice, forming a major water-traffic corridor
3.8 km long, 30 to 90 m wide, average depth 5 m
Reverse-S shape through the central sestieri, from near Santa Lucia station to the San Marco basin

w: A cluster of islands stitched together by bridges north of Venice, Murano was once its own comune before being folded into the city. Its name is shorthand worldwide for glass - furnaces here have shaped molten sand into art for centuries, watched over by a population that still barely tops five thousand.
s: The lagoon island that gave the world glass
_facts: Series of islands linked by bridges in the Venetian Lagoon, 1.5 km north of Venice
Famous for glass making
Population just over 5,000 (2004 figures)
Once an independent comune, now a frazione of Venice

w: Venice's answer to the plague was a bet with God: survive this and the city would build a basilica in thanks. The devastating 1630 epidemic brought Baldassare Longhena's domed Baroque landmark, anchoring the skyline since, painted again and again by Canaletto, Guardi and Turner.
s: A basilica built as a bet with God after the plague
_facts: Built as a votive offering after the devastating 1630 plague outbreak
Designed by Baldassare Longhena in the Baroque style, construction began 1631
Most recent of Venice's plague churches; objects inside reference the Black Death
Its dome became emblematic of Venice, painted by Canaletto, Guardi, Turner and Sargent

w: Burned to the ground three times, rebuilt three times - La Fenice earned its name, 'the Phoenix', the hard way. The 1996 fire was arson, gutting everything but the exterior walls; it reopened in 2004. Rossini, Bellini, Donizetti and Verdi all premiered work here.
s: Burned down three times, rose from the ashes each time
_facts: Historic opera house, one of the most renowned landmarks in the history of Italian theatre and opera
Destroyed by fire in 1774, 1836, and by arson in 1996; rebuilt each time, reopened 2004
Premieres by Rossini, Bellini, Donizetti and Verdi; conductors including Toscanini, Bernstein, Karajan, Abbado, Muti

w: A slender island in the Venetian Lagoon, Giudecca sits just across the water from Dorsoduro and is technically folded into that sestiere on the map - its own island, its own name, administered as somebody else's neighbourhood.
s: Venice's own island, filed under someone else's name
_facts: Island in the Venetian Lagoon
Part of the sestiere of Dorsoduro, a locality of the comune of Venice

w: Gilt and polychrome once coated every inch of this Grand Canal palazzo, earning it the name 'House of Gold' long before the gold wore off. Restored by Baron Giorgio Franchetti and given to the state in 1927, it's now reckoned Venice's best-surviving Gothic palazzo, tracery borrowed straight from the Doge's Palace.
s: The Grand Canal's gilded Gothic showpiece
_facts: Palace on the Grand Canal, named 'House of Gold' for its gilt and polychrome decoration
Designed by Marino Contarini, restored by Baron Giorgio Franchetti, became a museum in 1927
Regarded as the best-surviving palazzo of Venetian Gothic architecture
Facade uses window tracery and quatrefoil forms drawn from the Doge's Palace

w: Another plague, another vow: after a major outbreak, Venice thanked God with Andrea Palladio's waterfront church, built on Giudecca and dominating its skyline since. Inside hang works by Tintoretto, Veronese and Bassano - payment, in a sense, for a deliverance the city believed it had earned.
s: Palladio's plague church, dominating Giudecca's skyline
_facts: 16th-century votive church built to thank God for deliverance from a plague outbreak
Designed by Andrea Palladio, on the waterfront of Giudecca island
Contains paintings by Tintoretto, Paolo Veronese and Francesco Bassano

w: Plain brick outside, packed with Venice's dead and its greatest art inside - the Frari holds doges' tombs, a Donatello sculpture and two Titian altarpieces, including the Assumption still on the high altar. It's also the last church in the city to keep its rood screen intact.
s: Doges, Donatello and two Titians behind plain brick
_facts: One of the largest churches in Venice, a minor basilica in Campo dei Frari
Built of brick in Venetian Gothic style; contains many doges' tombs
Sculpture by Donatello; Titian's Assumption of the Virgin and Pesaro Madonna
Only church in Venice to retain its rood screen in place

w: Andrea Palladio's white marble basilica glows across the water from the Piazzetta di San Marco, and has done since 1610 - the single most photographed silhouette on the Venice skyline that isn't actually in central Venice, but on its own island a short crossing away.
s: Palladio's white marble basilica across the water
_facts: 16th-century Benedictine church, designed by Andrea Palladio, built 1566-1610
Renaissance basilica on its own island, opposite the Piazzetta di San Marco
Forms the focal point of the view from the Riva degli Schiavoni

w: Built in 1453 for doge Francesco Foscari on the widest bend of the Grand Canal, this Gothic palazzo has hosted centuries of Venetian spectacle - it's still the finish line for the Regata Storica every year, when a floating grandstand called La Machina goes up so officials can watch the race the way the doges once did.
s: A doge's Gothic palace, still the regatta finish line
_facts: Gothic palace built in 1453 for doge Francesco Foscari, designed by Bartolomeo Bon
Sits on the widest bend of the Grand Canal
Site of the finishing line and prize-giving for the annual Regata Storica

w: A Baroque-turned-Rococo palazzo on the Grand Canal, kept almost exactly as the 18th century left it - ceilings by Tiepolo, canvases by Guardi, enough gilt furniture to feel like a period piece. It's now the city's dedicated museum of the Settecento, one of eleven civic museums.
s: An 18th-century Venice palazzo frozen in its own era
_facts: Palazzo and art museum on the Grand Canal, noted example of Venetian baroque and rococo architecture
Displays paintings by Francesco Guardi and Giambattista Tiepolo
Public museum dedicated to 18th-century Venice, one of 11 venues of the Fondazione Musei Civici di Venezia

w: Tucked a few streets behind St Mark's, this 15th-century former monastic church was built by the Republic itself and dedicated to Zechariah, father of John the Baptist - the kind of scale and gravity that hints at how much the state once had riding on the monastery it stood beside.
s: A state-built church a few streets behind St Mark's
_facts: 15th-century former monastic church in Campo San Zaccaria, near St Mark's Basilica
Dedicated to Zechariah, father of John the Baptist
Built by the Republic of Venice

w: Mussolini opened this causeway in 1933 as the Ponte Littorio, the only road ever built onto car-free Venice. It got a new name at war's end - Ponte della Liberta, 'Liberty Bridge' - marking the fall of the dictatorship it was built to glorify. Every car, bus and tram into the centre still crosses it.
_facts: Road bridge connecting Venice's historic centre to the mainland, the only vehicular access
Designed 1932 by Eugenio Miozzi, opened 1933 by Mussolini as Ponte Littorio
Renamed Ponte della Liberta at the end of WWII to mark the fall of fascism
3.85 km long, runs alongside the 1846 railway viaduct

w: Santiago Calatrava's glass-and-steel span landed amid furious protest in 2007 - the fourth bridge ever thrown across the Grand Canal, and the first new one in generations. Officially named for the Italian constitution's 60th anniversary, Venice just calls it the Calatrava Bridge, linking the station to Piazzale Roma.
s: Calatrava's controversial fourth Grand Canal bridge
_facts: Fourth bridge over the Grand Canal, designed by Santiago Calatrava
Installed 2007-2008 amid protest from politicians and the public
Connects Santa Lucia railway station to Piazzale Roma
Officially named for the 60th anniversary of the Italian constitution; known locally as the Calatrava Bridge
